title: Hydroxy compounds
objectives: Recall ways of making alcohols: hydration of alkenes, cold dilute KMnO₄ on alkenes (diols), hydrolysis of halogenoalkanes, reduction of aldehydes and ketones (NaBH₄ or LiAlH₄) and of carboxylic acids (LiAlH₄), and hydrolysis of esters
Classify alcohols as primary, secondary or tertiary
Describe the reactions of alcohols: combustion, with Na, substitution to halogenoalkanes, oxidation with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇, dehydration to alkenes and esterification with carboxylic acids
Describe the tri-iodomethane (iodoform) test for the CH₃CH(OH)– group
Explain why alcohols are weaker acids than water
prior: Electrophilic addition and KMnO₄ oxidation of alkenes (Chapter 14)
why: Alcohols sit in the middle of organic chemistry: they are made from alkenes and halogenoalkanes, and turn into aldehydes, ketones, acids, alkenes and esters. Telling primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols apart by their reactions is a favourite Paper 1 and Paper 2 skill.
intro: An alcohol contains the –OH (hydroxy) group bonded to an sp³ carbon. The O–H bond lets alcohols hydrogen bond, giving them higher boiling points than alkanes of similar Mr, and makes the small ones soluble in water.

blocks.h: Look at the carbon that carries the OH: bonded to one other carbon → primary (butan-1-ol); two → secondary (butan-2-ol); three → tertiary (2-methylpropan-2-ol). Methanol counts as primary.

blocks.wrong: NaBH₄ reduces carboxylic acids to alcohols.
blocks.right: Only LiAlH₄ is strong enough to reduce a carboxylic acid. NaBH₄ reduces aldehydes and ketones.

blocks.h: Alcohols burn cleanly: C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O. Ethanol is used as a fuel and fuel additive.

2CH₃CH₂OH + 2Na → 2CH₃CH₂O⁻Na⁺ + H₂. Fizzing is seen, but more gently than with water. Alcohols are weaker acids than water: the alkyl group pushes electron density onto the O (positive inductive effect), making RO⁻ less stable than OH⁻. So alcohols do not react with NaOH(aq).

KCl or NaBr + conc. H₂SO₄, heat
HX is made in the flask

blocks.h: Heat a carboxylic acid with an alcohol and a few drops of concentrated H₂SO₄ (catalyst): CH₃COOH + CH₃CH₂OH ⇌ CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ + H₂O. Name the alcohol part first: ethyl ethanoate. The C=O part of the ester comes from the acid.

Acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ is reduced from orange Cr₂O₇²⁻ to green Cr³⁺ when it oxidises an alcohol. The carbon carrying the OH must also carry an H atom.

items: Use [O] in equations: CH₃CH₂OH + [O] → CH₃CHO + H₂O; CH₃CH₂OH + 2[O] → CH₃COOH + H₂O.
The aldehyde can be distilled off because it has no O–H, so no hydrogen bonding: its boiling point is lower than the alcohol's.
Dichromate does not attack C=C bonds, so an unsaturated alcohol keeps its C=C.

blocks.q: An alcohol C₄H₁₀O is oxidised under reflux to C₄H₈O, which cannot be oxidised further. Identify the alcohol.
steps: C₄H₈O has lost 2 H only, so it is an aldehyde or ketone
reflux would turn an aldehyde into an acid, so it must be a ketone: butanone
butanone comes from the secondary alcohol
blocks.err: Choosing butan-1-ol, which would end up as butanoic acid (C₄H₈O₂) under reflux.

blocks.h: Heat with concentrated H₃PO₄ or H₂SO₄, or pass the vapour over hot Al₂O₃. H₂O is removed: an OH from one carbon and an H from the next carbon. CH₃CH₂CH₂OH → CH₃CH=CH₂ + H₂O.

items: If H can be lost from carbons on either side, you get structural isomers: butan-2-ol → but-1-ene and but-2-ene.
Check each alkene for E/Z isomers: but-2-ene exists as E and Z, so butan-2-ol gives three alkenes in total.
Pentan-3-ol is symmetrical: losing H from C2 or C4 gives the same pent-2-ene (E and Z).

blocks.h: Warm with alkaline I₂(aq) (iodine and NaOH). A pale yellow precipitate of CHI₃ (antiseptic smell) shows the group CH₃CH(OH)– (or CH₃CO– in aldehydes and ketones).

items: The iodine first oxidises CH₃CH(OH)R to CH₃COR; then the CH₃ is split off as CHI₃ and the rest becomes the carboxylate ion RCOO⁻.
Example: propan-2-ol → CHI₃ + CH₃COO⁻; butan-2-ol → CHI₃ + CH₃CH₂COO⁻.
Positive: ethanol (the only primary alcohol), propan-2-ol, butan-2-ol, pentan-2-ol. Negative: methanol, propan-1-ol, pentan-3-ol, tertiary alcohols.

blocks.wrong: Only secondary alcohols give the iodoform test.
blocks.right: The test needs the CH₃CH(OH)– group. Ethanol has it (CH₃CH₂OH), so it is positive even though it is primary; pentan-3-ol is secondary but negative.

blocks.name: alcmystery
blocks.title: Mystery alcohol
blocks.h: Run tests on an unknown alcohol and identify it.

summary: Classify alcohols by how many carbons are bonded to the C–OH carbon.
Make alcohols by hydration of alkenes, hydrolysis of halogenoalkanes, reduction (NaBH₄ for aldehydes/ketones; LiAlH₄ also for acids) and ester hydrolysis.
Na → H₂ + alkoxide; alcohols are weaker acids than water (alkyl groups destabilise RO⁻).
PCl₅ gives steamy HCl fumes; SOCl₂, PCl₃, HX and PBr₃/PI₃ also replace OH by a halogen.
Acid + alcohol, conc. H₂SO₄ catalyst, heat → ester + water.
K₂Cr₂O₇/H⁺ (orange → green): primary → aldehyde (distil) or acid (reflux); secondary → ketone; tertiary → no reaction.
Dehydration (conc. H₃PO₄/H₂SO₄ or hot Al₂O₃) → alkene(s); count E/Z isomers.
Alkaline I₂ → yellow CHI₃ with CH₃CH(OH)–; the rest becomes RCOO⁻.

flash.q: Product of a primary alcohol with K₂Cr₂O₇, distilling?
Product of a primary alcohol with K₂Cr₂O₇, reflux?
Product of a secondary alcohol with K₂Cr₂O₇?
Colour change when dichromate oxidises an alcohol?
Why are tertiary alcohols not oxidised?
flash.a: No H on the carbon bearing the OH

flash.q: Why are alcohols less acidic than water?
flash.a: Alkyl group donates electrons, destabilising RO⁻
Conc. H₃PO₄ or H₂SO₄, heat; or vapour over hot Al₂O₃

flash.q: Which primary alcohol gives a positive iodoform test?
Name the ester from propanoic acid and methanol.

practice.q: Write equations, using [O], for the oxidation of propan-1-ol to (a) propanal and (b) propanoic acid, and give the conditions for each.
practice.a: (a) CH₃CH₂CH₂OH + [O] → CH₃CH₂CHO + H₂O, distil off as it forms; (b) CH₃CH₂CH₂OH + 2[O] → CH₃CH₂COOH + H₂O, heat under reflux with excess K₂Cr₂O₇/H₂SO₄.

practice.q: Describe a test to distinguish pentan-2-ol from pentan-3-ol.
practice.a: Warm with alkaline I₂(aq): pentan-2-ol gives a pale yellow precipitate (CHI₃); pentan-3-ol gives none.

practice.q: Name all the alkenes formed when butan-2-ol is dehydrated.
Write the equation for the formation of methyl ethanoate and give the conditions.
practice.a: CH₃COOH + CH₃OH ⇌ CH₃COOCH₃ + H₂O; heat with a few drops of concentrated H₂SO₄.

practice.q: Explain why ethanol reacts more slowly with sodium than water does.
practice.a: The ethyl group donates electron density to O, so the ethoxide ion is less stable than hydroxide; ethanol releases H⁺ less readily (weaker acid).

practice.q: Give the products of propan-2-ol with alkaline I₂(aq).

assessment.q: A secondary alcohol is oxidised to…
assessment.why: Only one H on the C–OH carbon.

assessment.q: Which gives a yellow precipitate with alkaline I₂?
Reaction of ethanol with sodium produces…
To obtain an aldehyde from a primary alcohol you should…
o: distil off the product as it forms

assessment.q: Which reagent reduces a carboxylic acid to an alcohol?
Which gas is seen as steamy fumes when PCl₅ is added to an alcohol?

assessment_s.q:
Three isomers C₄H₁₀O are P (butan-1-ol), Q (butan-2-ol) and R (2-methylpropan-2-ol).
(a) Classify each. [1]
(b) Which of P, Q and R turn warm acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ green? Name the organic product formed by Q. [2]
(c) Which gives a yellow precipitate with alkaline I₂(aq)? Name the two products. [2]
(d) Give the conditions to convert P into butanal and explain why they work. [2]
assessment_s.a:
(a) P primary, Q secondary, R tertiary
(b) P and Q; butanone
(c) Q; CHI₃ and propanoate, CH₃CH₂COO⁻
(d) warm with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ and distil off the product as it forms; butanal has a lower boiling point (no H-bonding) so it escapes before being oxidised to butanoic acid

assessment_s.q:
Propan-2-ol can be made from propene.
(a) Give the reagent and conditions. [2]
(b) Propan-2-ol is heated with conc. H₃PO₄. Name the reaction type and the product. [2]
(c) Write an equation for the reaction of propan-2-ol with ethanoic acid and name the ester. [2]
assessment_s.a:
(a) steam, H₃PO₄ catalyst, about 300 °C and 6 MPa
(b) dehydration (elimination); propene
(c) CH₃COOH + (CH₃)₂CHOH ⇌ CH₃COOCH(CH₃)₂ + H₂O; propan-2-yl (1-methylethyl) ethanoate

pp.skill: Which route gives a secondary alcohol
pp.mis: Thinking H adds to the CH carbon so OH goes on the end
pp.stem: Which reaction gives a secondary alcohol as the major organic product?
opts: propene with steam and H₃PO₄ catalyst
ethene with cold dilute acidified KMnO₄
pp.exp: Steam adds via the more stable secondary carbocation, giving propan-2-ol. LiAlH₄ reduces the acid to butan-1-ol and NaBH₄ reduces ethanal to ethanol (both primary); cold KMnO₄ gives ethane-1,2-diol (primary OH groups).

pp.skill: Choosing reactions that give a primary alcohol
pp.mis: Confusing elimination and substitution conditions
pp.stem: Which reaction has propan-1-ol as its major organic product?
opts: propene reacted with steam and H₃PO₄
pp.exp: NaBH₄ reduces an aldehyde to a primary alcohol: CH₃CH₂CHO + 2[H] → CH₃CH₂CH₂OH. Steam gives mainly propan-2-ol, ethanolic NaOH gives propene, and propanone gives propan-2-ol.

pp.skill: Following a three-step sequence
pp.mis: Forgetting Markovnikov addition in the last step
pp.stem: Butanoic acid is reduced with LiAlH₄ to give X. X is heated with concentrated H₂SO₄ to give Y. Y is passed with steam over H₃PO₄ to give Z (major product). What is Z?
pp.exp: X = butan-1-ol; Y = but-1-ene (dehydration); hydration of but-1-ene goes via the secondary carbocation, so OH ends up on C2: butan-2-ol.

pp.skill: Which reagents react with an alcohol
pp.mis: Thinking alcohols react with NaOH like acids
pp.stem:
Which reagents react with propan-2-ol?
1 sodium
2 aqueous sodium hydroxide
3 acidified potassium dichromate(VI), warm
pp.exp: Na displaces H₂ from the O–H. Propan-2-ol is a secondary alcohol, so it is oxidised to propanone. Alcohols are weaker acids than water, so they do not react significantly with NaOH(aq).

pp.skill: Reactions of alcohols that release HCl
pp.mis: Thinking sodium gives an acidic gas
pp.stem:
Four reagents are added separately to propan-1-ol at room temperature.
1 sodium
2 phosphorus(V) chloride
3 thionyl chloride, SOCl₂
4 aqueous sodium bromide
Which give off a gas that turns damp blue litmus paper red?
pp.exp: PCl₅ and SOCl₂ both replace OH by Cl and give off HCl (SOCl₂ also gives SO₂): acidic, steamy fumes. Sodium gives H₂, which is neutral; NaBr(aq) does not react.

pp.skill: Moving the functional group to a tertiary carbon
pp.mis: Using chlorine, which does not react with an alkene to give one Cl
pp.stem: 2-methylpropan-1-ol is converted into 2-chloro-2-methylpropane with reagent M followed by reagent N. Which is correct?
opts: M concentrated H₃PO₄, heat; N HCl(g)
pp.exp: M dehydrates the alcohol to methylpropene. HCl then adds via the tertiary carbocation, giving (CH₃)₃CCl. Cl₂ would add two Cl atoms; NaOH does not dehydrate an alcohol.

pp.skill: What can be deduced with certainty from tests
pp.mis: Over-concluding from a negative oxidation test
pp.stem: Compound T burns completely to give CO₂ and H₂O only. T fizzes with sodium. Warm acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ stays orange with T. What can be deduced with certainty?
pp.exp: Fizzing with Na shows an O–H group. No oxidation fits a tertiary alcohol but also a carboxylic acid, so neither can be stated for certain; nothing tells us about C=C.

pp.skill: Tertiary alcohols resist oxidation but still react with Na
pp.mis: Choosing a ketone, which does not react with Na
pp.stem: Which compound reacts with sodium but is not oxidised by warm acidified potassium dichromate(VI)?
pp.exp: 2-methylbutan-2-ol is tertiary: no H on the C–OH carbon, so it is not oxidised, but its O–H still reacts with Na. Butanone has no O–H; the primary and secondary alcohols are oxidised.

pp.skill: Spotting the alcohol that gives a different observation
pp.mis: Thinking secondary alcohols are not oxidised
pp.stem: Each compound is warmed with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇. Which gives a different observation from the other three?
pp.exp: 1-methylcyclohexanol is tertiary, so the solution stays orange. The others are primary or secondary alcohols, which are oxidised: orange → green.

pp.skill: Number of possible oxidation products
pp.mis: Forgetting that primary alcohols can stop at the aldehyde
pp.stem: Each alcohol is oxidised with Cr₂O₇²⁻/H⁺. For which can just a single organic product ever be obtained, whatever the conditions?
pp.exp: Secondary alcohols give only a ketone (pentan-3-one). Primary alcohols can give an aldehyde (distil) or a carboxylic acid (reflux); a tertiary alcohol gives none.

pp.skill: Identifying an alcohol from the composition of its oxidation product
pp.mis: Assuming every product under reflux is an acid
pp.stem: An alcohol U is heated with hot acidified K₂Cr₂O₇. The organic product contains 62.1% C, 10.3% H and 27.6% O by mass. What is U?
pp.exp: Ratio C : H : O = 62.1/12.0 : 10.3/1.0 : 27.6/16.0 = 5.17 : 10.3 : 1.73 = 3 : 6 : 1, so C₃H₆O: propanone, from propan-2-ol. Propan-1-ol under these conditions gives propanoic acid (C₃H₆O₂); butan-2-ol gives butanone (66.7% C).

pp.skill: Using Mr to identify an alcohol that forms an ester with its own acid
pp.mis: Choosing a secondary alcohol
pp.stem: Compound X has Mr = 74. X is heated under reflux with excess acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ to give Y. Y reacts with X, with a little concentrated H₂SO₄, to give Z with Mr = 144. What is X?
pp.exp: Butan-1-ol (74) → butanoic acid (88). Ester: 74 + 88 − 18 = 144 (butyl butanoate). Butan-2-ol gives a ketone, which cannot form an ester; the tertiary alcohol is not oxidised; propanoic acid is not oxidised.

pp.skill: Mass of acid from an oxidation with a percentage yield
pp.mis: Stopping at the aldehyde under reflux
pp.stem: 3.00 g of propan-1-ol is heated under reflux with excess acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ and the product is collected. The yield is 80.0%. [Mr: C₃H₈O, 60.0; C₃H₆O, 58.0; C₃H₆O₂, 74.0] What mass of product is collected?
pp.exp: Under reflux with excess oxidant the product is propanoic acid. n = 3.00 ÷ 60.0 = 0.0500 mol; 0.0500 × 74.0 × 0.800 = 2.96 g. (2.32 g would be propanal.)

pp.skill: Hydration then oxidation
pp.mis: Putting the OH on C1 after hydration
pp.stem: Propene reacts with steam in the presence of phosphoric acid. The major product is then heated under reflux with excess acidified K₂Cr₂O₇. What is the final organic product?
pp.exp: Hydration gives mainly propan-2-ol (secondary), which is oxidised to the ketone propanone. A ketone is not oxidised further.

pp.skill: Dichromate oxidises OH groups but leaves C=C alone
pp.mis: Treating dichromate like hot KMnO₄
pp.stem: Hex-4-en-2-ol, CH₃CH=CHCH₂CH(OH)CH₃, is heated with an excess of acidified K₂Cr₂O₇(aq). What is formed?
pp.exp: The secondary OH becomes C=O (ketone). Dichromate does not attack the C=C, so the chain is not split and no diol forms; that is what KMnO₄ would do.

pp.skill: Reaction types in an alcohol → diol route
pp.mis: Calling the first step reduction
pp.stem: Butan-2-ol is converted into butane-2,3-diol in two steps: step 1 heat with concentrated H₃PO₄; step 2 shake with cold dilute acidified KMnO₄. What types of reaction are these?
opts: step 1 elimination of H₂; step 2 hydration
pp.exp: Loss of H₂O gives but-2-ene (dehydration). Cold dilute KMnO₄ adds two OH groups across C=C (oxidation).

pp.skill: Which alkenes form from dehydration
pp.mis: Thinking H can be lost from any carbon
pp.stem:
Three alkenes are listed.
1 pent-1-ene
2 (Z)-pent-2-ene
3 (E)-pent-2-ene
Which can be formed by dehydrating pentan-3-ol?
pp.exp: OH is on C3, so H is lost from C2 or C4; both give pent-2-ene, as E and Z isomers. Pent-1-ene would need the C=C between C1 and C2.

pp.skill: All the products of dehydrating a secondary alcohol
pp.mis: Forgetting the stereoisomers
pp.stem: Pentan-2-ol is heated with concentrated H₂SO₄. Which list contains all the alkenes that can form?
pp.exp: H can go from C1 (pent-1-ene) or C3 (pent-2-ene). Pent-2-ene has different groups on both C=C carbons, so it exists as E and Z isomers.

pp.skill: Dehydration over Al₂O₃ then bromine addition
pp.mis: Putting the Br atoms on C1 and C3
pp.stem: Butan-1-ol vapour is passed over hot aluminium oxide. The hydrocarbon formed reacts with bromine. What is the product?
pp.exp: Dehydration gives but-1-ene (CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃). Br₂ adds across the C=C: CH₂BrCHBrCH₂CH₃.

pp.skill: Products of the tri-iodomethane reaction
pp.mis: Keeping all the carbons in the carboxylate
pp.stem: Alcohols are warmed with alkaline I₂(aq). Which row is correct?
pp.exp: CH₃CH(OH)R is oxidised to CH₃COR, then the CH₃ becomes CHI₃ and the rest becomes RCOO⁻. For butan-2-ol, R = C₂H₅: propanoate. Butan-1-ol has no CH₃CH(OH) group; propan-2-ol gives ethanoate.

pp.skill: An oxidation product that gives the tri-iodomethane test
pp.mis: Forgetting that ethanal (and ethanol) also contain CH₃C–
pp.stem: X is oxidised (and the product distilled off) to give Y. Y gives a yellow precipitate with alkaline I₂(aq). What could X be?
pp.exp: Ethanol → ethanal, CH₃CHO, which has the CH₃C=O group, so it gives CHI₃. Methanal and propanal do not have a CH₃ next to C=O; the tertiary alcohol is not oxidised.

pp.skill: Identifying an alcohol from its oxidation product and the iodoform test
pp.mis: Choosing the symmetrical secondary alcohol
pp.stem: Q, C₅H₁₂O, is oxidised to R, C₅H₁₀O. R gives a yellow precipitate with alkaline I₂(aq). What is Q?
pp.exp: R must be a methyl ketone, CH₃COC₃H₇ (pentan-2-one), so Q is pentan-2-ol. Pentan-3-ol gives pentan-3-one (no CH₃CO); pentan-1-ol gives pentanal; the tertiary alcohol is not oxidised.

pp.skill: Pairs that give different results with alkaline I₂
pp.mis: Thinking only ketones give the test
pp.stem: In which pair do the two compounds give different visible results with alkaline I₂(aq)?
pp.exp: Ethanal (CH₃CHO) gives a yellow precipitate; propan-1-ol has no CH₃CH(OH) group, so it does not. In the other pairs both compounds contain CH₃CH(OH)– or CH₃CO– and both give the precipitate.

pp.skill: Choosing a reagent to tell two alcohols apart
pp.mis: Choosing a reagent that reacts with every alcohol
pp.stem: Reagent X is added separately to butan-1-ol and to 2-methylpropan-2-ol. The visible results are different. What is X?
pp.exp: Butan-1-ol (primary) turns dichromate green; the tertiary alcohol leaves it orange. Na and PCl₅ react with both; neither alcohol has a CH₃CH(OH) group, so alkaline I₂ gives no precipitate with either.

pp.skill: Distinguishing a primary from a secondary alcohol
pp.mis: Using dichromate, which is reduced by both
pp.stem: Which test distinguishes butan-1-ol from butan-2-ol?
pp.exp: Only butan-2-ol has CH₃CH(OH)–, so only it gives yellow CHI₃. Both alcohols turn dichromate green, fizz with Na and give fumes with PCl₅.

pp.skill: Counting alcohols that give the tri-iodomethane test
pp.mis: Forgetting optical isomers
pp.stem: Count every isomer, including optical isomers. Of all the alcohols C₄H₁₀O, how many form CHI₃ when warmed with iodine and NaOH(aq)?
pp.exp: Of the four C₄H₁₀O alcohols, only butan-2-ol contains CH₃CH(OH)–. Its C2 is chiral, so there are two enantiomers: 2.

pp.skill: A diol that gives a dicarboxylic acid with alkaline I₂
pp.mis: Choosing a diol with only one CH₃CH(OH) end
pp.stem: Y reacts with alkaline I₂(aq). After acidifying, the organic product is a dicarboxylic acid HOOC–R–COOH, where R is one or more CH₂ groups. What is Y?
pp.exp: CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₂CH(OH)CH₃ has CH₃CH(OH)– at both ends. Each end loses its CH₃ as CHI₃ and becomes COO⁻, giving HOOCCH₂CH₂COOH (butanedioic acid). Hexane-1,5-diol reacts at one end only.

pp.skill: Which acid and alcohol make a given ester
pp.mis: Swapping the acid and alcohol parts
pp.stem: Which pair could react to give the ester CH₃COOCH₂CH₂CH₃?
pp.exp: The part with C=O (CH₃CO–) comes from the acid: ethanoic acid. The –O–CH₂CH₂CH₃ part comes from the alcohol: propan-1-ol. The ester is propyl ethanoate.

pp.skill: Formula of an ester from an acid and an alcohol
pp.mis: Writing the alcohol part next to the C=O
pp.stem: Methanoic acid reacts with ethanol, with concentrated H₂SO₄ as catalyst. What is the formula of the organic product?
pp.exp: RCOOH + R′OH → RCOOR′ + H₂O. With R = H and R′ = C₂H₅: ethyl methanoate, HCOOCH₂CH₃.

pp.skill: Classifying alcohols and predicting test results
pp.stem: Alcohols can be classified and identified by simple tests.

parts.q: Classify 3-methylpentan-3-ol, CH₃CH₂C(OH)(CH₃)CH₂CH₃, and explain your answer.
ms: tertiary: the C bearing OH is bonded to three other C atoms

parts.q: Butan-2-ol is tested with three reagents. Give the observation for each: (i) Na, (ii) warm acidified K₂Cr₂O₇, (iii) warm alkaline I₂(aq).
Give the observations for 3-methylpentan-3-ol with the reagents in (ii) and (iii).
ms: no reaction with either: stays orange; no precipitate

pp.skill: Making an alcohol and oxidising it to an acid
pp.stem: Butan-1-ol can be made from 1-chlorobutane and then oxidised to butanoic acid.

parts.q: State the reagent and solvent needed to convert 1-chlorobutane into butan-1-ol.
Butan-1-ol is heated under reflux with acidified potassium dichromate(VI). State the colour change.
Write an equation for the oxidation, using [O] for an oxygen atom from the oxidising agent.
How would you change the method to obtain butanal instead? Explain.
ms: distil the product off as it forms (and use limited oxidising agent)
the aldehyde has a lower boiling point (no hydrogen bonding), so it leaves before it can be oxidised further

pp.skill: Hydration of an alkene and the acidity of alcohols
pp.stem: But-1-ene reacts with steam in the presence of H₃PO₄: C₄H₈(g) + H₂O(g) → C₄H₁₀O(g).

parts.q: Draw or write the structures of the two alcohols that can form, and state which is the major product.
ms: butan-2-ol is major (via the more stable secondary carbocation)

parts.q: Explain why alcohols are less acidic than water.
ms: the alkyl group donates electron density (positive inductive effect) to the O
so the RO⁻ ion is less stable than OH⁻ / its negative charge is more concentrated, so RO–H releases H⁺ less readily

parts.q: Write an equation for the reaction of butan-2-ol with sodium.
